verdicts.text: Pulumi Neo is built around a loop of proposing infrastructure changes, running previews, and executing approved updates with policy guardrails in place.
verdicts.evidence: The Neo docs describe each part of the loop: it "Proposes changes to your code", "Runs previews before anything lands", and the task modes gate `pulumi up`: "Review mode (default): Neo requires approval before running `pulumi preview`, running `pulumi up`, and opening a pull request." The overview says Neo "adds organizational context, policy guardrails, human-in-the-loop approvals".
verdicts.framing_note: The docs list proposing changes, previews, approval-gated `pulumi up`, and policy guardrails as separate capabilities. The claim describes them together as one loop, which is a reasonable summary. The docs also say the usual output is a pull request, not a direct update.

verdicts.text: That gap between trust and guardrails is exactly what a supervised, agentic operating model has to close: an agent that proposes a change, runs a preview, and waits for approval, rather than one that only writes YAML for someone else to apply by hand. [Pulumi Neo](https://www.pulumi.com/product/neo/
verdicts.evidence: The cited URL returns HTTP 200 and is the right target: "Pulumi Neo - Your AI Infrastructure Agent … Meet Neo, our AI-powered infrastructure engineering agent". The pre-fetched text was cut off after the navigation menu, so it doesn't show the claimed workflow of proposing a change, running a preview and waiting for approval.
verdicts.framing_note: The page confirms Neo is an "AI infrastructure agent". The supervised preview-and-approval detail doesn't appear in the fetched text. This is also a pulumi.com page, so it could only back up the claim, not settle it on its own authority.

verdicts.text: Kubernetes is evolving in response to AI demands, requiring low-latency execution closer to the user for inference workloads powered by LLMs and GPUs.
verdicts.evidence: This is editorial trend commentary in a predictions blog, not a checkable Pulumi product or feature claim. The linked anchor exists in the sibling post ("## The 2026 Convergence of AI, Platforms, and Policy in Kubernetes"), which says "AI and ML workloads are becoming first-class citizens in Kubernetes environments." It does not mention low-latency or edge inference. The low-latency part is the author's own general industry framing, with no source cited.
verdicts.framing_note: The linked Pulumi post backs up "evolving in response to AI demands" but not "low-latency execution closer to the user"; the second half is the author's own framing.

verdicts.text: [Kubernetes is also evolving in response to AI demands](https://www.pulumi.com/blog/beyond-yaml-kubernetes-2026-automation-era/#the-2026-convergence-of-ai-platforms-and-policy-in-kubernetes), a shift Pulumi covers in more depth in its [comparison of Kubernetes IaC tools](https://www.pulumi.com/blog/
verdicts.evidence: The cited page loads (HTTP 200) and its title is "Beyond YAML in Kubernetes: The 2026 Automation Era | Pulumi Blog". The fetched text was cut off after the site navigation, so I couldn't quote the section on Kubernetes evolving for AI. Only the URL fragment (#the-2026-convergence-of-ai-platforms-and-policy-in-kubernetes) suggests that section exists.
verdicts.framing_note: This is a link to another Pulumi blog post. The link works and the anchor name matches the claim, but the part of the page that would support the claim wasn't in the fetched text.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A blog post about 2024 trends links to a post about 2026. Check that the timeline wording in the surrounding text still makes sense.

verdicts.text: AI-powered coding assistants like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Cursor have moved from novelty to everyday tooling for a large share of enterprise software teams.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Independent surveys back the qualitative claim. The Stack Overflow 2025 survey found "51% of professional developers use AI tools daily." JetBrains 2025 found 85% of developers use AI regularly and 62% rely on an assistant or agent. JetBrains' January 2026 AI Pulse put Copilot at 29% work use and Cursor and Claude Code at 18% each. A secondary source adds that "90% of Fortune 100 companies use GitHub Copilot."
verdicts.source: https://www.getpanto.ai/blog/ai-coding-assistant-statistics ; https://www.secondtalent.com/resources/ai-coding-assistant-statistics/ ; WebSearch ran query "enterprise developers AI coding assistants adoption survey 2025"
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is vague and qualitative ("a large share of enterprise software teams"), and the survey data supports it. The evidence comes from secondary aggregator sites summarizing Stack Overflow and JetBrains surveys, which is why confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: According to Gartner, 63% of organizations are currently piloting, deploying, or beginning to use AI code assistants.
verdicts.evidence: Gartner's April 11, 2024 press release confirms the 63% figure: "Sixty-three percent of organizations are currently piloting, deploying or have already deployed AI code assistants" (Q3 2023 survey of 598 respondents). The claim changes the third group from "have already deployed" to "beginning to use".
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source says 'piloting, deploying or have already deployed'; the claim says 'piloting, deploying, or beginning to use'. That downplays full deployment and drops the survey scope (598 global respondents, Q3 2023). Minor fix: use the source's wording.

verdicts.text: The July 2026 revision of the Model Context Protocol is described by its maintainers as the largest revision of the protocol to date.
verdicts.evidence: In the official MCP blog post announcing the 2026-07-28 spec release candidate, the maintainers write: "It is the largest revision of the protocol since launch." WorkOS and Developers Digest also attribute this description to the maintainers.
verdicts.framing_note: Source: "largest revision of the protocol since launch"; claim: "largest revision of the protocol to date". These mean the same thing. The spec is dated July 28, 2026, which matches the claim's "July 2026 revision".

verdicts.text: AWS shipped a general-availability MCP server for its Agent Toolkit.
verdicts.evidence: AWS What's New (May 2026): "Today, AWS announces the general availability of the AWS MCP Server" and it "is a core component of the Agent Toolkit for AWS."
verdicts.framing_note: AWS names the product "Agent Toolkit for AWS"; the claim's "its Agent Toolkit" means the same thing.

verdicts.text: Mirantis's Lens, a Kubernetes tooling vendor, has launched a built-in MCP server connecting AI coding assistants to Kubernetes.
verdicts.evidence: The Mirantis press release (March 18, 2026) says "Lens by Mirantis today announced the launch of a built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) server in Lens Desktop." Its headline is "Lens Launches Built-In MCP Server Connecting AI Coding Assistants to Kubernetes," and it names Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor and GitHub Copilot as supported assistants.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim follows the release's headline wording. Small nit: Lens is a product (a Kubernetes IDE) and Mirantis is the vendor, so calling "Lens" a "vendor" is slightly loose.

verdicts.text: As enterprise adoption of AI assistants increases, expectations are rising: they must not only generate code but also understand the state of infrastructure, configurations, and security posture. verdicts.text: Pulumi Agent Skills teaches tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI to reason about Pulumi projects, reducing hallucination and improving outputs based on real infrastructure conventions and practices.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's launch post calls Agent Skills "packaged expertise that teaches any AI coding assistant how to work with Pulumi the way an experienced practitioner would." It lists Claude Code, Cursor and Gemini CLI among the supported platforms. The "reducing hallucination" part is a fair paraphrase of "correct, idiomatic Pulumi guidance," not something the source says outright.
verdicts.framing_note: Source: "teaches any AI coding assistant" and lists "Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI". The claim names three of those tools, so it's a special case. The "reducing hallucination" benefit is marketing-style wording the source only implies.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Remote MCP Server provides infrastructure access that lets teams build secure, AI-driven workflows where assistants provide insights and Pulumi Neo safely executes actions with previews, policies, and orchestration.
verdicts.evidence: The cited Remote MCP Server announcement says it lets assistants "instantly access your Pulumi Cloud infrastructure... and delegate complex automation tasks to Pulumi Neo", and that "your AI assistant identifies *what* needs to be done, and Neo *does* it", with human-in-the-loop approval and policy-violation fixes. The claim's "previews, policies, and orchestration" is a loose summary of that page, which mentions testing, policy compliance, and multi-step planning rather than previews by name.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says the assistant "identifies what needs to be done, and Neo does it"; the claim phrases this as "assistants provide insights and Neo safely executes actions". Only a Pulumi blog post supports this, so it is not independent product source.

verdicts.text: Modern IaC, unified governance, reusable components, and policy frameworks are all core capabilities of the Pulumi Cloud platform.
verdicts.evidence: The docs home lists all four as platform capabilities: "Infrastructure as Code", "Discovery & governance — Search, compliance, and policy enforcement across your cloud infrastructure", and "Internal Developer Platform — Self-service infrastructure with templates, guardrails". Reusable components come through the IDP and private registry offerings.
verdicts.framing_note: Small wording issue: Pulumi IaC is the open-source SDK/CLI, not strictly part of "Pulumi Cloud". The claim is accurate for the Pulumi platform as a whole.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is marketing positioning. Calling "modern IaC" a Pulumi Cloud capability blurs the line between the OSS engine and the SaaS product.
